items.title: You Don't Need Animations
items.summary: Emil Kowalski argues that most interface animations should be cut: they only earn their keep when they explain something, give feedback, or land a rare delight moment, and anything a user triggers many times a day is usually better instant.
items.why: A crisp craft note from the animation practitioner Manik already rates highest — directly useful as a rule of thumb inside CueDesign when reviewing motion on high-frequency actions in the learner app, where every 300ms of ceremony compounds against pace.

items.title: Now Linear writes the code, too
items.summary: Linear ships Coding Sessions, automated triage and a native diff view so its agent can go from an issue to a pull request inside Linear itself — pitched as making AI a shared team capability rather than a solo productivity hack.
items.why: The clearest picture yet of what an agent-native product tool looks like from the most design-led shop in the category — a live reference for how the design and PM loop at Cuemath could be re-shaped around shared agent context, not private prompt sessions.

items.title: UX Roundup: UX Benchmark | Impact of AI Mentions | Character Design Workflow
items.summary: Nielsen's weekly digest leads with UXBench findings — AI models that ace technical benchmarks still fail on usability, with verbosity alone driving over a third of bad experiences and only 12% recovery when users express frustration — plus a two-stage cheap-then-expensive workflow for generating character video.
items.why: Concrete numbers to bring into the argument that 'the model is smart' is not the same as 'the product is usable' — useful ammunition for keeping UX rigor in the design × AI conversation at Cuemath, and the two-stage generation workflow is a directly copyable pattern for kids' character work.

items.title: How Freitag keeps its cool: inside the brand's less-than-conventional campaigns
items.summary: Creative director Thomas Wakeford walks through how Freitag builds campaigns from the bag outward — casting real customers and employees instead of models, letting shoots stay unpredictable, and refusing demographic targeting.
items.why: A working playbook for a brand that stays distinctive for decades without trend-chasing — useful reference as Cuemath pushes its brand system beyond a logo into campaign work, where casting real learners and staying craft-first over polish-first would land.

items.title: Altera Italia by Alessia Rollo
items.summary: Artist book set in Rapida (by Italian type designer Michelangelo Nigra), designed by Grupppo — exposed-spine binding that lies flat, upside-down type, dotless lowercase i's and coarse paper stock treated as part of the argument, not decoration.
items.why: A high-craft reminder that editorial typography carries meaning through decisions most readers never consciously notice — the exact sensibility to keep sharpening for Cuemath's own editorial and workbook surfaces where structure and texture do half the teaching.
